analysis.one_liner: Blocks the IRS from hiring enforcement staff until its taxpayer service improves.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop the IRS from hiring anyone for enforcement work — auditors, examiners, investigators — until its phone service hit strict targets for six straight months, 90% of staff worked on-site, and its backlog and refund delays shrank. It would also lock audit rates for taxpayers with incomes under $400,000 at their most recent pre-2023 levels. The practical effect is to delay or shrink IRS enforcement staffing, which falls hardest on complex, high-income returns.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers with taxable incomes under $400,000 would be guaranteed no increase in audit rates over their most recent pre-bill year. In practice, the biggest beneficiaries would be high earners and others with complex returns, because that is where added enforcement staffing would otherwise be directed — wealthy households are audited far more than their share of filings when the IRS has the resources. Large employers and aggressive filers also benefit from a smaller enforcement workforce.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the IRS from hiring any enforcement personnel until it has maintained, for 6 consecutive months, 90% phone-line access, an average call answer time of 4 minutes or less, and 90% of employees working in person [S2][S3].

Barred the IRS from auditing taxpayers with taxable incomes below $400,000 at a higher rate than in the most recent taxable year before enactment, a shield aimed at middle- and upper-middle-income filers [S2][S3].

Also blocked nearly all other hiring — everything except return processing and call center staff — until the IRS processed its backlog down to 5 million cases and issued refunds within six weeks [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Honest, compliant taxpayers and the Treasury, if the bill passed: less enforcement means more taxes go uncollected, and the shortfall is made up by people who do pay what they owe. Taxpayers trying to reach the IRS would also live with a smaller agency, since the bill ties any staffing growth to service targets rather than adding staff to fix the service itself.
analysis.who_pays_short: Compliant taxpayers and the U.S. Treasury

drawbacks.text: The audit-rate freeze is written against a single baseline year, locking in whatever audit rate under-$400,000 filers faced at that moment, which makes it hard for the IRS to redirect enforcement even if data later shows a compliance problem in a specific group [S3].

The enforcement-hiring freeze applies to all exam and collection staff regardless of funding, so an agency already losing staff to retirement would shrink while its workload — including returns from high earners — went unexamined; independent estimates put uncollected taxes in the hundreds of billions per year, and the shortfall is effectively paid by filers who report honestly (general knowledge).

Requiring 90% of employees on-site before any hiring is allowed to resume ties workforce growth to a condition unrelated to the enforcement work being frozen, and could be difficult to meet during any disruption (in-person requirement per the bill text) [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated aim — better phone service and faster refunds — is something every taxpayer wants, and the audit-rate floor gives under-$400,000 filers real protection from rate increases. But the way it is written trades those goals against the government's ability to collect taxes it is already owed: the hiring freezes would reduce the enforcement workforce that pays for itself many times over, and the heaviest toll would land on complex, high-income compliance, with honest filers absorbing the difference. A bill that genuinely fixed customer service would add the staff to do it, not withhold them.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. John Thune introduced the bill on April 27, 2023, with Sen. Susan Collins as its only cosponsor [S1][S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance that same day; that was the last action on the bill [S5].
No committee action, floor vote, or further step appears in the record for the remainder of the 118th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never passed, the IRS kept its existing enforcement capacity rather than having hiring frozen. Honest taxpayers benefit from enforcement that remains intact; the people who would have gained from the bill — high earners facing scrutiny on complex returns — did not.

for.name: Sen. John Thune
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on April 27, 2023.

for.name: Sen. Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor listed.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the committee took no action on it after referral.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call exists; the bill had two Republican sponsors and the Senate's Democratic majority took no action on it after referral.

industries.note: Freezing enforcement hiring and audit rates for under-$400,000 incomes means the enforcement that would otherwise land on complex, high-income returns does not happen. Noncompliance at the top is effectively carried by compliant taxpayers and the Treasury.

The bill would freeze hiring for enforcement and nearly all other functions until service and backlog targets were met, shrinking an agency already losing staff to retirement. An adequately staffed IRS is what delivers the faster refunds and better phone service the bill says it wants.
